paragraphs: About 150 people in Ireland have small weather stations at home. They measure things like temperature and rain. They send this data to a website called Wow. Met Éireann, the national weather service, uses the data.
But Wow will close in December. The UK Met Office built it. It says the technology is too old now.
Met Éireann wants to keep the network. It is working with other EU countries on a new website. It hopes to start it in early 2027.
Schools and sports clubs also have stations. A good station costs a few hundred euro. Met Éireann says local data helps. Weather in Ireland can change a lot over short distances.
Users should download their old data before December.

Around 150 weather fans in Ireland run small weather stations at their homes, schools and clubs. They send their readings to a website called Wow, and Met Éireann, the national weather service, uses this information. Now the network is in danger.
Wow was built by the UK Met Office, which says the technology is too old to support. The website will close in December, and the data will not move to a new system.

Met Éireann is working with other EU countries on a new platform. It hopes to launch it in early 2027, so there may be a short gap without a service. It has asked users to download any old data they want to keep.

The stations are not official, because the equipment is very different from place to place. Met Éireann has 25 official stations. However, Noel Fitzpatrick, who leads its observations work, says the amateur stations fill gaps and help to follow storms.
Sean Rima, a weather lover in Co Galway, looks after 10 stations in the west. He says the weather can be very different only a few kilometres away.

Met Éireann is racing to keep a network of about 150 amateur weather stations alive after the UK platform that collects their data announced it will shut down. The stations, run by individuals, schools, sports clubs and some public bodies, send readings to the Weather Observations Website, known as Wow.
The UK Met Office, which created Wow, says its ageing technology can no longer be supported, so the service will close in December. Existing data will not be transferred to any replacement.

Met Éireann is working with other EU states on a new platform and is cautiously aiming to launch it in early 2027 to keep the gap in service as short as possible. Users are being encouraged to download their historical records before the closure.

The amateur data is not treated as official, because the equipment varies too much to be checked consistently. Met Éireann's 25 official stations remain the backbone of its network. Even so, Noel Fitzpatrick, its acting head of observations, says the extra stations fill gaps and are useful for tracking weather fronts and severe weather, as Ireland's landscape causes big local differences.
Enthusiasts such as Sean Rima in Connemara, who manages 10 stations, say a decent station costs only a couple of hundred euro.

Met Éireann is scrambling to salvage a grassroots network of some 150 amateur weather stations, after the British platform that hosts their readings announced it would be switched off. Maintained by hobbyists, schools, sports clubs and a handful of public bodies, the stations feed data into the Weather Observations Website, or Wow.

The UK Met Office, which devised Wow, has concluded that its antiquated technology is no longer viable, and the service will be decommissioned in December. Crucially, none of the accumulated data will migrate to a successor system.

In response, Met Éireann has joined forces with other EU states to develop a new platform, which it is tentatively hoping to unveil in early 2027. In the interim, contributors are being urged to download any archived records they wish to preserve.

Because the equipment is so heterogeneous, the amateur readings cannot be rigorously quality-controlled and are not deemed official; the 25 official stations remain the cornerstone of the national network. Nonetheless, Noel Fitzpatrick, the acting head of observations, contends that the volunteer stations plug gaps in coverage and prove invaluable for tracking fronts and severe weather, given how markedly conditions can diverge across Ireland's varied terrain.
Devotees such as Sean Rima, who oversees 10 stations in Connemara, note that a reliable station costs a mere couple of hundred euro.

Met Éireann is endeavouring to preserve a network of approximately 150 amateur weather stations, following the announcement that the platform which collects their data is to be discontinued. These stations, which are operated by private individuals, schools, sports clubs and several public bodies, transmit observations to the Weather Observations Website (Wow).

The UK Met Office, which developed the platform, has stated that its outdated technology can no longer be maintained; consequently, the service will cease operating in December. Furthermore, existing data will not be transferred to any subsequent system.

Met Éireann is collaborating with other EU member states to establish an alternative platform, with a provisional launch date in early 2027, in order to minimise any disruption. In the meantime, users have been advised to download historical data that they wish to retain.

Although the amateur observations are not classified as official, owing to substantial variation in equipment, they constitute a valuable supplement to the 25 official stations. According to Noel Fitzpatrick, the acting head of observations, such stations compensate for gaps in coverage and facilitate the monitoring of severe weather, particularly since Ireland's topography produces considerable local variation.
Nevertheless, the long-term viability of the network will be contingent upon the successful development of the new platform.
